nameStory: The Broad-tailed Hummingbird gets its name from the male's distinctively wide tail feathers, which are noticeably broader than those of its close relatives. When the male flies, these broad tail feathers create a unique metallic trilling sound that acts like a built-in musical instrument, making this species as much heard as seen.
description: The Broad-tailed Hummingbird is a medium-sized hummingbird typically found in the mountainous regions of western North America. Males sport brilliant rose-red throats (called gorgets) that flash like jewels in the sunlight, while females are more subdued with greenish backs and pale, lightly spotted underparts. They're about 4 inches long with wingspans reaching nearly 5 inches. This western mountain specialist is an extremely rare vagrant to New England, with only one recorded observation in our region.

idTips.label: Male's metallic wing trill
idTips.description: Males produce a distinctive high-pitched, metallic trilling sound in flight that sounds like a tiny cricket or electrical buzzing - you'll often hear them before you see them

idTips.label: Male's rose-red throat
idTips.description: Adult males have brilliant rose-red to magenta throat patches that appear to glow like neon in direct sunlight but can look nearly black in shadow

idTips.label: Broad tail shape
idTips.description: The tail appears noticeably wide and squared-off compared to other hummingbirds, especially obvious when the bird hovers or fans its tail while feeding

idTips.label: Female's spotted throat
idTips.description: Females have white to pale buff throats with small dark spots scattered across them, creating a lightly speckled appearance

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Medium-sized for a hummingbird with a relatively stocky build and straight, black bill that's neither particularly long nor short

habitat: In New England, you would only encounter this species as an extremely rare vagrant, most likely at hummingbird feeders in yards or gardens during migration periods. Any sighting would be exceptional and newsworthy for local birding communities. In their normal western range, they prefer mountain meadows and forest edges at high elevations.

seasonality.spring: Extremely unlikely to appear in New England during spring migration. Any spring sighting would be extraordinary and should be carefully documented with photos.
seasonality.summer: Not expected in New England during summer breeding season, as they nest exclusively in western mountains.
seasonality.fall: Fall migration offers the only realistic chance for a vagrant to appear in New England, though this would still be exceptionally rare.
seasonality.winter: Does not occur in New England during winter, as the species migrates to Mexico and Central America.

funFact: The male's wing trill is so distinctive that researchers can identify individual birds by the unique pitch and quality of their wing music - each male essentially has his own signature tune that he carries wherever he flies!
confusionNotes: In the extremely unlikely event you see one in New England, the metallic wing trill of males is the key feature that separates them from Ruby-throated Hummingbirds. Remember: if you hear that cricket-like buzzing from a hummingbird, you're witnessing something very special.
contextualKnowledge: This species represents one of those 'holy grail' sightings for New England birders - a western vagrant that would generate excitement throughout the regional birding community. Always photograph any hummingbird that doesn't look quite right, as documentation is crucial for such rare occurrences.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Rufous Hummingbird (another western species), male Broad-tailed Hummingbirds have rose-red rather than orange-red throats and lack the extensive rufous coloring on the back and sides. The wing trill is also distinctly different - Broad-tailed males produce a continuous metallic buzz while Rufous males make more of a choppy buzzing sound.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its close relatives, the rufous hummingbird is the only Selasphorus species regularly recorded in New England, making identification easier.
Compared to its Selasphorus relatives like Rufous and Allen's Hummingbirds, the Calliope is much smaller and males have the unique streaky throat pattern instead of solid-colored gorgets.
Allen's Hummingbird is nearly identical to the Rufous Hummingbird, with males showing slightly more orange tones in their throat patches versus the Rufous's more intense red-orange.
